A_target.statement:
In [[Definition:Type Theory|type theory]], the type $\mathbf 2$ of [[Definition:Boolean|booleans]], with constants $\mathsf {true}$ and $\mathsf {false}$ and its case analysis principle, is equivalent to:
:$\mathbf 2 \simeq \mathbf 1 + \mathbf 1$
with case analysis given by the [[Definition:Eliminator|eliminator]] of the [[Definition:Sum Type|sum type]].

B_source.statement:
Let $A$ and $B$ be [[Definition:Type|types]].
The [[Definition:Sum Type|sum type]] $A + B$ has introduction rules $\mathsf {inl}: A \to A + B$ and $\mathsf {inr}: B \to A + B$, and eliminator:
:$\mathsf {case}: \paren {A \to C} \to \paren {B \to C} \to \paren {A + B \to C}$

derived.the dependent eliminator: proof by case analysis on a boolean

validity_conditions: The unit type has exactly one element, so a sum of two copies has exactly two, matching the booleans.
The two injections become the two constants, and the sum eliminator becomes the conditional, since a function out of the unit type is determined by a single value.
The dependent form of the eliminator is needed to prove properties of an arbitrary boolean; the simple conditional alone does not give the case-analysis principle.
proof_plan:
A [[Definition:Mapping|function]] $\mathbf 1 \to C$ is determined by a single value $c \in C$.
Hence the eliminator specializes to:
:$\mathsf {case}: C \to C \to \paren {\mathbf 1 + \mathbf 1 \to C}$
